question: For finite noisy observations generated by a simple closed-form expression, when does Bayesian description length stop identifying that exact expression and favor simpler alternatives?

key_findings.claim: The paper casts symbolic model discovery as posterior inference over expression trees and approximates each model's negative log joint probability by half its BIC minus the log of a learned expression prior.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 1-4 marginalize parameters, use a Laplace/BIC approximation, and interpret the resulting H(m) as joint data-and-model description length; the Bayesian machine scientist samples expression trees with Metropolis moves.

anchors.section: Equations 1-4, model posterior and description length

key_findings.claim: When generating expressions from the same prior used for inference, the minimum-description-length expression predicts near the irreducible noise floor at low and high noise, with its largest relative generalization error near the model-identification transition.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 varies sample count and Gaussian observation noise for two synthetic expressions, compares test RMSE with the noise scale, and reports a peak in scaled RMSE where the posterior landscape contains multiple plausible expressions.

key_findings.claim: The empirical learnability fraction drops sharply with noise and collapses approximately across the two expressions and sample sizes when noise is divided by an analytic crossover estimate.
key_findings.evidence: For each noise level and N, 40 datasets are declared learnable when the true expression is the sampled MDL model; Figures 2-3 show the change from the true model to simple high-prior models and scaled curve collapse.

key_findings.claim: Equating the expected description lengths of the true expression and the most probable a-priori trivial expression yields a noise crossover that grows with sample size and approximates the observed transition.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 8-9 express the threshold through the reducible variance, sample count, parameter count, and prior description-length gap; because the estimate diverges as N grows, any fixed noise becomes learnable asymptotically under consistency assumptions.

key_findings.claim: The phrase 'unlearnable by any method' is conditional on the chosen model universe, prior, and data-only decision rule: another scientifically justified prior or side information can change which structure is identifiable and where the crossover occurs.
key_findings.evidence: Learnability is operationally defined as the true model being MAP/MDL under p(m), while the methods explicitly say quantitative thresholds depend on the prior and the true-generating model is sampled from that prior in the principal experiment.

anchors.section: Bayes optimality under the generating prior

key_findings.claim: The neural-network comparison does not establish a fundamental limitation of standard machine learning: it uses one small four-by-ten ReLU architecture and early-stopping recipe against an oracle-aligned symbolic prior.
key_findings.evidence: The methods specify two inputs, four hidden layers of ten units, validation stopping, and three repeats; no capacity-matched search, alternative activations, interpolation method, or uncertainty-calibrated neural baseline is tested.

method.core_idea: View closed-form structures as statistical-mechanical configurations whose energy is Bayesian description length, then locate the noise level where a simple high-prior expression overtakes the generating expression.
method.mechanism: Place a corpus-learned maximum-entropy prior over expression-tree operators, approximate parameter marginalization with BIC, sample the posterior with expression-tree MCMC, select the MDL model, and compare expected H(m*) and H(m_c) to estimate a sample-size/noise crossover.
assumptions: The true mapping is an expression in the enumerated closed-form grammar and its parameters are identifiable.
Inputs are low dimensional, observations are IID, and additive Gaussian noise is an adequate model.
The likelihood is locally peaked and the parameter prior smooth enough for the BIC/Laplace approximation.
The expression prior reflects the relevant scientific model distribution.
MCMC explores the posterior well enough to find all expressions more plausible than the known generating expression.
The transition estimate is dominated by the true and highest-prior trivial models away from the hard region.

techniques.role: Defines probability over symbolic structures after marginalizing continuous parameters.
Approximates model evidence and balances data fit against parameter and expression complexity.
Samples candidate closed forms by local structural edits.
Measures how often the known generator is the MDL expression across noisy dataset realizations.
Approximates the transition by equating the description lengths of true and trivial models.

evaluations.setting: Two synthetic two-variable closed-form generators drawn from the Bayesian-machine-scientist prior
evaluations.metric: Test RMSE divided by observation noise over N in {25,50,100,200,400}
evaluations.result: MDL prediction approaches the irreducible noise floor at low/high noise and has a relative-error peak in the crossover region.
evaluations.baseline: Four-by-ten ReLU ANN and random forest

evaluations.setting: Forty random datasets per noise level for each generator and sample size
evaluations.metric: Fraction for which the generator is the MDL expression
evaluations.result: Learnability falls from near one to near zero as noise rises and approximately collapses under the analytic rescaling s_epsilon/s_epsilon_cross.

Low noise concentrates on the generator, high noise on trivial models, and the transition contains a multiplicity of alternative expressions with lower description length than either simple endpoint approximation.
evaluations.baseline: True expression and maximum-prior trivial expression

limitations: The main experiments use only two low-dimensional synthetic equations, chiefly drawn from the same prior used for inference.
The operational transition is prior- and grammar-dependent rather than an assumption-free identifiability boundary.
BIC can be inaccurate for singular, weakly identifiable, small-sample, or multimodal parameter models.
Posterior MCMC may miss a more plausible expression, making empirical learnability optimistic.
The analytic bound ignores other competing expressions that are demonstrably important near the transition.
Neural and random-forest baselines are narrow and not evidence of general non-symbolic limits.
failure_modes: A misspecified grammar excludes the scientific law and converts structure recovery into approximation selection.
Correlated, heteroscedastic, adversarial, or input-dependent noise invalidates the Gaussian description-length threshold.
Equivalent expressions split posterior mass and make exact syntax recovery look unlearnable despite semantic recovery.
A corpus prior favors conventional short expressions and suppresses a novel but true law.
Expression-tree MCMC becomes trapped and reports a search transition rather than an information transition.
reusable_insights: Separate exact syntax recovery, algebraic-equivalence recovery, predictive accuracy, and scientific intervention validity.
Report learnability curves over data size and noise instead of only symbolic-regression success at one benchmark point.
Stress-test structure conclusions across plausible priors, grammars, noise models, and equivalent-expression canonicalizations.
Use posterior mass or calibrated credible sets of expressions near the hard region rather than a single winning formula.
Benchmark search failure with posterior enumeration on small grammars before interpreting it as fundamental impossibility.
open_questions: Can prior-robust lower and upper identifiability bounds be derived for equivalence classes of expressions?
How does the transition change under colored noise, latent variables, interventions, or active experimental design?
Can symbolic and neural models share a fair predictive/complexity prior for out-of-grammar generators?
How much of the hard region is statistical ambiguity versus expression-search mixing time?
Can experiment selection move a system across the learnability boundary more efficiently than collecting IID points?

competitive_landscape.title: A Bayesian machine scientist to aid in the solution of challenging scientific problems
competitive_landscape.difference: The predecessor introduces the corpus-learned expression prior and posterior MCMC; this paper uses that machinery to study sample/noise identifiability transitions and analytic crossover scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: AI Feynman: a Physics-Inspired Method for Symbolic Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: AI Feynman exploits symmetry, separability, and neural approximation to recover formulas; the present work emphasizes Bayesian uncertainty, priors, and an information/noise boundary rather than raw recovery rate.

competitive_landscape.title: Discovering Governing Equations from Data by Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
competitive_landscape.difference: SINDy selects sparse terms from a fixed candidate library for dynamics; the Bayesian machine scientist searches compositional expression trees and the limit analysis covers static closed-form regression under a learned grammar prior.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Symbolic Regression: Recovering Mathematical Expressions from Data via Risk-Seeking Policy Gradients
competitive_landscape.difference: Deep Symbolic Regression trains a recurrent generator to optimize expression reward; this paper samples a Bayesian posterior and can represent ambiguity, but its transition inherits a particular grammar and prior.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Closed-form model discovery exhibits a noise-driven learnable-to-unlearnable phase transition whose location can be estimated from Bayesian description lengths, with probabilistic selection quasi-optimal away from the hard region.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Two synthetic model families show sharp learnability curves, scaled collapse, description-length switching, and an analytic true-versus-trivial crossover near the empirical transition.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The transition lens and scaling diagnostic are valuable for symbolic-regression evaluation. It is a Bayesian, prior-relative boundary rather than a universal data-only impossibility theorem, and broader grammars, noise processes, search audits, and fairer predictive baselines are needed.
